title: Two (of Many) Things I'm (Intentionally) Not Good At
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a conversation about teacher stress and burnout, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that much of the profession's overload could be relieved if teachers gave themselves explicit permission to be only "minimally effective" in areas outside their chosen few priorities — the same logic behind picking the six focus areas in These 6 Things. To make the principle concrete, he names two things he deliberately does not excel at: replicating full lesson content for absent students (he simply points them to the lesson slide and lets them recover notes and handouts from peers) and maintaining a "perfect" gradebook (he keeps classwork intentionally low-stakes and accepts that late grading, while imperfect, matters far less to learning than late feedback). In both cases he weighs the marginal benefit of doing the task well against the real cost in personal time and stress, and concludes the cost isn't justified. The piece closes by reframing this selective mediocrity as professionalism rather than laziness: finite human beings improve fastest by majoring on the majors and consciously settling for "good enough" everywhere else.
points: Stuart's core burnout-mitigation strategy is explicit permission to be "minimally effective" in chosen areas, treating finite time and energy as a real constraint rather than something to feel guilty about.
His first confessed weak spot — not replicating full lesson content for absent students — trades a small amount of student convenience for real hours of at-home labor he judges not worth it.
His second confessed weak spot — an imperfect, low-stakes gradebook — is built on the claim that late feedback harms learning far more than late grading does.
He explicitly separates "far from perfect" from "terrible," arguing that satisficing in secondary areas is compatible with genuine professionalism, not a lapse from it.
The essay models vulnerability as a teaching-life genre: naming specific professional shortcomings publicly rather than only prescribing best practices.
quotes: Though the teaching workload today is unambiguously stressful and overloaded, much of that stress and overload could be mitigated if we gave ourselves permission to be minimally effective in certain areas of our job.
Would doing those things I just listed make me a better teacher? Perhaps. Are they valuable enough to justify the extra hours (at home) I'd need to take to make them possible?
The thing with my gradebook is, I want the student's final grade to look like the students' actual degree of mastery of the course material.
Late grading isn't nearly as big a problem for student learning as late feedback is. The biggest problem with late grading is that it can end up annoying me and annoying my students.
It's actually very professional to major on the majors like I describe in These 6 Things and The Will to Learn. Professionals aren't perfect — they're smart, capable, wise, and improving every year.
